chunks: Why I2C rise time is too slow. The question: Why would rise time be too slow on I2C?
I2C is a two-wire connection that lets chips talk. After a chip stops pulling a wire low, a resistor pulls it back up. The "rise time" is how long that climb takes.
If it is too slow, the data goes wrong, usually at higher speeds.
This page is about finding out why it is slow: either the resistor is too big, the wire holds too much charge, or an extra part on the bus adds charge or resistance.
Imagine pumping up a bike tire through a thin straw. The straw is the pull-up resistor, and the tire is the capacitance of the wire and everything attached. A thin straw is slow.
A bigger tire is slow too. Time the inflation, check the straw, and you can work out the tire size.
The back-calculation of C b splits the problem. If the capacitance is bigger than the budget, find the extra picofarads.
If it isn't, the resistor is the problem or something is adding series resistance.
Rise time: time for the wire to go from 30% to 70% of the supply voltage. Pull-up resistor: the resistor that pulls the wire up to the supply.
Bus capacitance: the charge the wire, cables and chips soak up as the voltage changes. Internal pull-up: a weak resistor built into a microcontroller pin.
Its resistance is much too high to be useful at I2C speeds.
Rise time is about 0. 85 times R times C . Suppose a bus has a 10 kilohms pull-up and 100 picofarads. That gives about 850 nanoseconds.
A 400 kilohertz bus needs 300 nanoseconds or less, so it fails, though it might work at 100 kilohertz. Now run it backward.
If you measure 420 nanoseconds and know the resistor is 4. 7 kilohms, then C equals 420 nanoseconds over (0. 85 times 4700) about 105 picofarads.
If that is far more than the parts add up to, something else adds capacitance. That is the whole idea.
"Rise time is about 0. 85 times R p times C b , so slow means too much R, too much C, or something extra in the path.
On the R side: pull-up too big, only internal pull-ups, pull-up on the wrong rail, or a series resistor.
On the C side: too many devices, a cable or connector, big ESD parts, or the scope probe.
I measure the 30-to-70% rise, back out the capacitance from the known pull-up, and compare it with my budget."
